notes.definition: The digestive system is an organ system in which several organs work together to digest and absorb food. Digestive enzymes break large insoluble food molecules into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream.
explanation: Food contains large molecules (starch, proteins and lipids) that are too big and insoluble to pass through the wall of the small intestine. The digestive system breaks them down and absorbs the products. Food passes from the mouth, down the oesophagus, to the stomach, then the small intestine (where most digestion is completed and products are absorbed) and the large intestine (where water is absorbed). The salivary glands, pancreas, liver and gall bladder add secretions along the way.

Enzymes are biological catalysts: they speed up reactions without being used up. They are large protein molecules, and each has a uniquely shaped region called the active site. In the lock and key model, only a substrate with a complementary shape fits the active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex. The reaction happens and the products are released, leaving the enzyme unchanged. This is why each enzyme catalyses only one specific reaction.

Temperature and pH affect enzyme activity. As temperature increases, molecules move faster and collide more often, so the rate increases up to an optimum (about 37 °C for human enzymes). Above the optimum, bonds holding the enzyme in shape break, the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits: the enzyme is denatured, and this is permanent. Each enzyme also has an optimum pH; a pH too far from it also changes the shape of the active site and denatures the enzyme.

Carbohydrases such as amylase break down carbohydrates (starch) into simple sugars. Amylase is made in the salivary glands, the pancreas and the small intestine. Proteases break proteins into amino acids; they are made in the stomach, the pancreas and the small intestine. Lipases break lipids (fats and oils) into fatty acids and glycerol; they are made in the pancreas and the small intestine. The products are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, and some glucose is used in respiration.

Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder before being released into the small intestine. Bile is alkaline, so it neutralises the hydrochloric acid that comes from the stomach, giving the slightly alkaline conditions in which pancreatic and intestinal enzymes work best. Bile also emulsifies fats, breaking large drops into many small droplets. This increases the surface area for lipase to act on. Both effects increase the rate of fat digestion.

Required practical 4 (food tests): Benedict's reagent tests for sugars (heat in a water bath; blue turns green, yellow or brick-red depending on the amount of sugar). Iodine solution tests for starch (orange-brown turns blue-black). Biuret reagent tests for protein (blue turns purple). Lipids can be shown with Sudan III, which stains lipids red and forms a red layer on top. Required practical 5: the effect of pH on amylase is found by timing how long it takes for starch to disappear (iodine no longer turns blue-black) at different pH values using buffer solutions.
keyFacts: Enzymes are biological catalysts made of protein.
The active site has a specific shape complementary to one substrate (lock and key model).
High temperature and extreme pH denature enzymes by changing the shape of the active site.
Amylase: starch → sugars; made in salivary glands, pancreas and small intestine.
Protease: protein → amino acids; made in stomach, pancreas and small intestine.
Lipase: lipids → fatty acids + glycerol; made in pancreas and small intestine.
Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder and released into the small intestine.
Bile neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fat into small droplets (larger surface area).
Stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) gives the low pH that stomach protease needs and kills many microorganisms.
Food tests: Benedict's (sugars), iodine (starch), Biuret (protein), Sudan III (lipids).
Rate of reaction can be calculated as 1 ÷ time, or as amount of product formed ÷ time.

keyTerms.definition: A protein that acts as a biological catalyst, speeding up a reaction without being used up.
The region of an enzyme with a specific shape where the substrate binds.
The molecule an enzyme acts on.
Permanently changed in shape, so the substrate no longer fits the active site and the enzyme cannot work.
The temperature or pH at which an enzyme works fastest.
An enzyme that breaks down carbohydrates into simple sugars, for example amylase.
An enzyme that breaks down proteins into amino acids.
An enzyme that breaks down lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.
An alkaline liquid made by the liver that neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fats.
To break large fat drops into many small droplets, increasing their surface area.

equations.name: Rate of reaction (from amount)
equations.formula: rate = amount of product formed (or substrate used) ÷ time

workedExamples.question: Lipase produced 1.8 g of fatty acids in 3 minutes. Calculate the rate of reaction in g per second.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think enzymes are killed at high temperatures.
misconceptions.right: In fact enzymes are molecules, not living things. They are denatured: the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think bile is an enzyme that digests fat.
misconceptions.right: In fact bile contains no enzymes. It emulsifies fat (increasing surface area for lipase) and neutralises stomach acid.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think low temperatures denature enzymes.
misconceptions.right: In fact at low temperatures enzymes work slowly because there are fewer collisions, but their shape is not changed, so activity returns when warmed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think bile is made in the gall bladder.
misconceptions.right: In fact bile is made in the liver; the gall bladder only stores it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think digestion happens mainly in the stomach.
misconceptions.right: In fact the stomach begins protein digestion, but most digestion is completed, and nearly all absorption happens, in the small intestine.

realWorld: Biological washing powders contain proteases and lipases that digest food and grease stains at low wash temperatures.
People whose gall bladder is removed may struggle to digest fatty meals because bile is released less effectively.
Food manufacturers test products for sugar, starch and protein content using reactions similar to the classroom food tests.
People with pancreatic conditions such as cystic fibrosis may take enzyme capsules with meals to help digestion.
examTips: Never say enzymes are 'killed'. Say 'denatured' and explain that the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits.
When naming where an enzyme is made, give the organ (for example pancreas), not the place it acts.
For bile, give both functions: neutralises acid and emulsifies fat, and link emulsifying to increased surface area for lipase.
In food test questions, give the reagent, the starting colour and the positive result colour.
In rate questions, show 1 ÷ time and include units (s⁻¹).
summary: The digestive system is an organ system that digests and absorbs food.
Enzymes are protein catalysts with a specific active site (lock and key).
Temperature and pH affect enzyme activity; extremes denature enzymes.
Carbohydrases, proteases and lipases produce sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol.
Bile neutralises acid and emulsifies fats, speeding up fat digestion.
Food tests: Benedict's, iodine, Biuret, Sudan III. Rate = 1 ÷ time.

flashcards.back: The substrate has a shape complementary to the active site, so it fits and forms an enzyme-substrate complex; products are released and the enzyme is unchanged.
The active site has permanently changed shape so the substrate no longer fits.

questions.question: What type of molecule are enzymes?
questions.explanation: Enzymes are large protein molecules folded into a specific shape.

questions.question: Which enzyme breaks down starch?
questions.explanation: Amylase is a carbohydrase. Lipase acts on lipids, protease on proteins, and bile is not an enzyme.

questions.question: What are the products of protein digestion?
questions.explanation: Proteases break proteins into amino acids. Fatty acids and glycerol come from lipids.

questions.question: Which reagent is used to test for starch?
questions.explanation: Iodine turns from orange-brown to blue-black with starch. Benedict's tests for sugars and Biuret for protein.

questions.question: Where is bile made?
questions.explanation: Bile is made in the liver and only stored in the gall bladder, which is the common wrong answer.

questions.question: Which organ produces amylase, protease and lipase?
questions.explanation: The pancreas makes all three groups. The stomach makes protease only; salivary glands make amylase; the liver makes bile.

questions.question: A student adds Biuret reagent to a food solution. What colour shows that protein is present?
questions.explanation: Biuret reagent turns from blue to purple (lilac) with protein. Brick-red is a positive Benedict's test and blue-black a positive iodine test.

questions.question: Why does emulsifying fat increase the rate of fat digestion?
options: It breaks fat into fatty acids and glycerol
It increases the surface area of fat for lipase to act on
It lowers the pH to the optimum for lipase
It increases the temperature of the small intestine
questions.explanation: Emulsification is physical: large drops become small droplets with more total surface area. It does not chemically digest the fat, and bile raises pH rather than lowering it.

questions.question: Why does an enzyme stop working when it is heated well above its optimum temperature?
options: The enzyme molecules are killed by the heat
The substrate molecules move too fast to bind
Bonds holding the enzyme's shape break, so the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits
The enzyme is used up in the reaction
questions.explanation: Denaturation changes the active site shape. Enzymes are not alive so cannot be killed, and catalysts are not used up.

questions.question: Stomach protease is added to a solution at pH 8. What will happen to its activity, and why?
options: Activity is high because protease works best in alkaline conditions
Activity is very low because pH 8 is far from its optimum of about pH 2, which changes the shape of the active site
Activity is unchanged because pH does not affect enzymes
Activity increases because more substrate collisions occur
questions.explanation: Stomach protease has an acidic optimum. At pH 8 its active site shape is altered so it cannot bind its substrate effectively.

questions.question: In an amylase experiment, starch had disappeared after 50 s. Calculate the rate of reaction using rate = 1 ÷ time.
questions.explanation: 1 ÷ 50 = 0.02 per second.

questions.question: Protease digested 2.4 g of protein in 4 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of reaction in g per minute.
questions.explanation: Rate = amount ÷ time = 2.4 ÷ 4 = 0.6 g/min.

questions.question: A student repeated the pH 6 amylase test three times. Starch disappeared after 60 s, 70 s and 80 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction, using rate = 1000 ÷ mean time. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: Find the mean time first: 210 ÷ 3 = 70 s. Then 1000 ÷ 70 = 14.29, which is 14.3 to 3 significant figures.

questions.question: At pH 7 amylase took 30 s to break down the starch. At pH 9 it took 120 s. Calculate the percentage decrease in the rate of reaction (rate = 1 ÷ time) when the pH was changed from 7 to 9.
questions.explanation: The time increased by a factor of 4, so the rate fell to one quarter of its value. A fall to 25% is a 75% decrease. A common error is to calculate the percentage change in time (300%) instead of rate.

questions.question: Lipase released fatty acids at a rate of 0.015 g/s. Calculate the mass of fatty acids produced in 2.5 minutes.
questions.explanation: Rearrange rate = amount ÷ time to amount = rate × time, after converting minutes to seconds: 0.015 × 150 = 2.25 g.

questions.question: Name the enzyme group that breaks down lipids and give the products.
questions.explanation: Lipases break lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.question: Describe how to test a food sample for sugar using Benedict's reagent, and give the positive result.
markScheme: 1 mark: add Benedict's reagent and heat in a (hot) water bath (about 75 °C) for a few minutes
1 mark: colour changes from blue to green / yellow / brick-red if sugar is present
questions.explanation: The mixture must be heated. The final colour depends on how much sugar is present: green for a little, brick-red for a lot.

questions.question: Explain why each enzyme can only catalyse one specific reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: the active site has a specific shape
1 mark: only a substrate with a complementary shape can fit into it (lock and key)
questions.explanation: The fit between active site and substrate is like a key in a lock. Other molecules have the wrong shape.

questions.question: Describe the two roles of bile in digestion.
markScheme: 1 mark: bile is alkaline and neutralises hydrochloric acid from the stomach
1 mark: giving the optimum pH for enzymes in the small intestine
1 mark: emulsifies fat into small droplets, increasing surface area for lipase
questions.explanation: Both roles increase the rate of fat digestion by lipase.

questions.question: Suggest why the products of digestion must be small and soluble.
acceptedAnswers: pass through wall of small intestine
markScheme: 1 mark: so they can be absorbed through the wall of the small intestine
1 mark: into the bloodstream (to be transported to cells)
questions.explanation: Large insoluble molecules cannot cross the intestinal lining, so they must be broken down first.

questions.question: In required practical 5, a student uses a buffer solution and a water bath. Give the reason for each.
markScheme: 1 mark: buffer: to keep the pH at the value being tested / control pH
1 mark: water bath: to keep the temperature constant, because temperature also affects enzyme activity
questions.explanation: pH is the independent variable, set by the buffer. Temperature is a control variable, kept constant so the test is fair.

questions.question: In required practical 5, a drop of the amylase-starch mixture is added to iodine on a spotting tile every 10 seconds. Explain how this allows the rate of reaction to be found and give one limitation of the method.
markScheme: 1 mark: when iodine no longer turns blue-black (stays orange-brown), all the starch has been broken down
1 mark: the time taken is recorded and rate calculated as 1 ÷ time
1 mark: limitation: sampling every 10 s means the end point is only known to within 10 s / judging the colour change is subjective
questions.explanation: The end point is when starch has gone. Because samples are taken at intervals, the true time could be up to 10 s earlier; using a colorimeter or shorter intervals improves precision.

questions.question: Explain why the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction increases between 20 °C and 37 °C but falls sharply above about 45 °C.
markScheme: 1 mark: as temperature rises, molecules have more kinetic energy so there are more (successful) collisions between enzyme and substrate
1 mark: so more enzyme-substrate complexes form per second
1 mark: above the optimum the enzyme is denatured: the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits
questions.explanation: The rise is about collision frequency; the fall is about loss of shape. Mentioning only one gives at most 2 marks.

questions.question: A student adds Sudan III to a mixture of food and water. A red layer forms on top. What does this show?
questions.explanation: Sudan III stains lipids red; lipids float, so a red layer appears on top.

questions.question: Which organ stores bile?
questions.explanation: The gall bladder stores bile made by the liver until it is released into the small intestine.

questions.question: A student finds that the rate of starch digestion by amylase is highest at pH 7. Which is the best conclusion?
options: The optimum pH is between pH 6 and pH 8 and further tests at smaller intervals are needed to find it precisely
Amylase works best in acidic conditions
questions.explanation: With pH values tested at intervals of 1 (for example 5, 6, 7, 8), the true optimum lies somewhere around the highest result. Smaller intervals would locate it more precisely.

questions.question: Describe how a student could test a sample of food to find out whether it contains starch, sugars and protein. (Required practical 4)
markScheme: Indicative content: grind food with distilled water using a pestle and mortar and filter or allow to settle; divide into test tubes; starch: add a few drops of iodine solution, orange-brown to blue-black if starch present; sugars: add Benedict's reagent, heat in a water bath at about 75 °C for 5 minutes, blue to green, yellow or brick-red if sugar present; protein: add Biuret reagent, blue to purple if protein present; safety: eye protection, care with hot water and Biuret reagent (contains copper sulfate and sodium hydroxide, which is corrosive).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear method for at least two tests with reagents and correct colour changes, including the need to heat for Benedict's.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): reagents named with some correct colours, but method unclear.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the sample preparation, the right reagent for each test, heating for Benedict's, and correct before and after colours.

questions.question: A meal contains starch, protein and fat. Explain how each of these is digested as the meal passes through the digestive system, including the roles of the organs that produce enzymes and bile.
markScheme: Indicative content: mouth: salivary glands release amylase, starch begins to be broken down to sugars; stomach: glandular tissue releases protease and hydrochloric acid; acid gives low pH optimum for stomach protease and kills microorganisms; muscular tissue churns food; proteins begin to be digested to amino acids (shorter chains); liver makes bile, stored in the gall bladder, released into the small intestine; bile neutralises acid and emulsifies fat to small droplets, increasing surface area; pancreas releases amylase, protease and lipase into the small intestine; small intestine also makes these enzymes; starch completed to sugars, protein to amino acids, fat to fatty acids and glycerol; products are small and soluble so are absorbed into the blood through the small intestine wall; used to build new molecules or glucose for respiration.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed, logically sequenced account of all three food types, naming enzymes, sites of production, products and the role of bile with explanation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes digestion of at least two food types with enzymes and products; some reference to bile or organs.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names some enzymes or products with little organisation.
questions.explanation: Strong answers follow the food along the gut, name where each enzyme is made, give products, and explain bile's two roles rather than just naming them.

questions.question: State the colour change when iodine solution is added to a solution containing starch.
questions.explanation: Iodine is orange-brown and turns blue-black in the presence of starch.
